abstract: Chiral organs such as the gut develop complex, stereotyped shapes, despite variability in the molecular and cellular processes that build them. How cell activity specifies tissue-scale handedness and reproducibly shapes whole organs remains unclear. Here, we use the embryonic Drosophila midgut to understand how a symmetric tubular organ reliably coils into a complex loop of alternating handedness, without any known left-right asymmetric gene expression.Through multi-view light-sheet imaging, 3D geometric analysis, and physical modeling, we show that midgut handedness is specified by epithelial cells in a neighboring organ, relayed across all three germ layers, and finally amplified and canalized by the mechanics of confined gut elongation. Myosin 1C expression in the hindgut epithelium controls midgut handedness up to hundreds of microns away, transmitting chiral bias to the midgut through migratory cells that form the longitudinal muscle. As the midgut elongates, a buckling instability then amplifies early left-right asymmetric constrictions, and confinement funnels the organ into a stereotyped coil. Tissue mechanics thus canalizes organ shape into one of two chiral forms, selected by an inter-organ cellular relay.
